exclusively inward. She saw unusual loiterers in the streets: men with
their hands in their pockets sauntering along; loud-laughing and
loud-spoken girls clustered together, apparently excited to high
spirits, and a boisterous independence of temper and behaviour. The more
ill-looking of the men—the discreditable minority—hung about on the
steps of the beer-houses and gin-shops, smoking, and commenting pretty
freely on every passer-by. Margaret disliked the prospect of the long
walk through these streets, before she came to the fields which she had
planned to reach. Instead, she would go and see Bessy Higgins. It would
not be so refreshing as a quiet country walk, but still it would perhaps
be doing the kinder thing.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret's revived spirits amid industrial Milton reveal class anxiety and initial resistance to working-class neighbourhoods, with attention to unusual street behaviour hinting at labour unrest.
enrichment.best_quote: She saw unusual loiterers in the streets: men with their hands in their pockets sauntering along; loud-laughing and loud-spoken girls clustered together, apparently excited to high spirits, and a boisterous independence of temper and behaviour.
enrichment.summary: Margaret goes out for a walk, notices the unusual presence of idle workers in Milton's streets, and decides to visit Bessy Higgins instead of going to the countryside.

text:
Nicholas Higgins was sitting by the fire smoking, as she went in. Bessy
was rocking herself on the other side.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief scene-setting with minimal action or dialogue; establishes the Higgins household and their current state.
enrichment.summary: Margaret enters the Higgins home to find Nicholas smoking by the fire and Bessy rocking herself on the other side.

text:
Nicholas took the pipe out of his mouth, and standing up, pushed his
chair towards Margaret; he leant against the chimney-piece in a lounging
attitude, while she asked Bessy how she was.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine courtesy and dialogue greeting; minimal narrative content.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas gestures Margaret to his chair and asks about Bessy's health.

text:
“Hoo’s rather down i’ th’ mouth in regard to spirits, but hoo’s better
in health. Hoo doesn’t like this strike. Hoo’s a deal too much set on
piece and quietness at any price.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas introduces the central topic of the chapter—the strike—while revealing Bessy's psychological opposition to conflict and labour unrest.
enrichment.best_quote: Hoo doesn't like this strike. Hoo's a deal too much set on piece and quietness at any price.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas observes that Bessy is upset by the strike and prefers peace, showing disagreement between father and daughter on labour action.

text:
“This is th’ third strike I’ve seen,” said she, sighing, as if that was
answer and explanation enough.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's weary comment reveals both her experience of repeated industrial unrest and her fatalism, hinting at her mortality and spiritual resignation.
enrichment.best_quote: This is th' third strike I've seen," said she, sighing, as if that was answer and explanation enough.
enrichment.summary: Bessy sighs that this is the third strike she has witnessed, implying a lifetime of labour turmoil.

text:
“Well, third time pays for all. See if we don’t dang th’ masters this
time. See if they don’t come and beg us to come back at our own price.
That’s all. We’ve missed it afore time, I grant yo’; but this time we’n
laid our plans desperate deep.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas expresses working-class militancy and determination, revealing the rhetorical power and optimism of strike action while hinting at past failures.
enrichment.best_quote: Well, third time pays for all. See if we don't dang th' masters this time. See if they don't come and beg us to come back at our own price.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas declares confidence that this strike will succeed in forcing the masters to capitulate and rehire workers at higher wages.

text:
“Why do you strike?” asked Margaret. “Striking is leaving off work till
you get your own rate of wages, is it not? You must not wonder at my
ignorance; where I come from I never heard of a strike.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret's naive question about strike mechanics introduces her as an outsider unfamiliar with labour struggle, establishing the pedagogical dynamic of the chapter.
enrichment.best_quote: Striking is leaving off work till you get your own rate of wages, is it not? You must not wonder at my ignorance; where I come from I never heard of a strike.
enrichment.summary: Margaret asks Nicholas to explain what a strike is, revealing her southern gentry background has no experience of industrial labour unrest.

text:
“I wish I were there,” said Bessie, wearily. “But it’s not for me to get
sick and tired o’ strikes. This is the last I’ll see. Before it’s ended
I shall be in the Great City—the Holy Jerusalem.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's declaration of her imminent death and anticipated heavenly relief is arresting and tragic, revealing both her illness and religious faith as escape from earthly suffering.
enrichment.best_quote: But it's not for me to get sick and tired o' strikes. This is the last I'll see. Before it's ended I shall be in the Great City—the Holy Jerusalem.
enrichment.summary: Bessy declares that she will not see another strike because she expects to die before this one ends, and anticipates entering heaven.

text:
“Hoo’s so full of th’ life to come, hoo cannot think of th’ present. Now
I, yo see, am bound to do the best I can here. I think a bird i’ th’
hand is worth two i’ th’ bush. So them’s the different views we take on
th’ strike question.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas contrasts his practical earthly focus with Bessy's otherworldly resignation, revealing philosophical differences on labour, duty, and hope amid family conflict.
enrichment.best_quote: Now I, yo see, am bound to do the best I can here. I think a bird i' th' hand is worth two i' th' bush.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas explains that he must act for immediate earthly justice while Bessy prefers to await heavenly reward.

text:
“But,” said Margaret, “if the people struck, as you call it, where I
come from, as they are mostly all field labourers, the seed would not be
sown, the hay got in, the corn reaped.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret raises a practical economic objection to strikes using southern agricultural labour as analogy, beginning her challenge to Nicholas's strike logic.
enrichment.best_quote: if the people struck, as you call it, where I come from, as they are mostly all field labourers, the seed would not be sown, the hay got in, the corn reaped.
enrichment.summary: Margaret argues that strikes in the agricultural South would harm food production and economic cycles.

text:
“Well?” said he. He had resumed his pipe, and put his “well” in the form
of an interrogation.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A single word of dialogue serving as transition; no substantive content.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas responds with a questioning 'well' to Margaret's point.

text: “Why,” she went on, “what would become of the farmers?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret pursues her economic logic with a question about farmers' survival, advancing her naive but sensible critique.
enrichment.summary: Margaret asks what would happen to farmers if workers struck in the South.

text:
He puffed away. “I reckon, they’d have either to give up their farms, or
to give fair rate of wage.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas's brief, dismissive response; establishes his impatience with Margaret's economic objections.
enrichment.best_quote: I reckon, they'd have either to give up their farms, or to give fair rate of wage.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas argues that farmers would have to choose between abandoning their farms or paying fair wages.

text:
“Suppose they could not, or would not do the last; they could not give
up their farms all in a minute, however much they might wish to do so;
but they would have no hay, nor corn to sell that year; and where would
the money come from to pay the labourers’ wages the next?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret develops a more sophisticated economic counter-argument about cash flow and debt cycles, showing her intelligence despite her ignorance of strikes.
enrichment.best_quote: they would have no hay, nor corn to sell that year; and where would the money come from to pay the labourers' wages the next?
enrichment.summary: Margaret challenges Nicholas by pointing out that without harvests to sell, farmers could not pay wages the following year.

text: Still puffing away. At last he said:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas pauses to smoke; minimal substantive content or development.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas continues smoking without immediate response.

text:
“I know nought of your ways down South. I have heerd they’re a pack of
spiritless, down-trodden men; welly clemmed to death; too dazed wi’
clemming to know when they’re put upon. Now, it’s not so here. We known
when we’re put upon; and we’en too much blood in us to stand it. We just
take our hands fro’ our looms, and say, ‘Yo’ may clem us, but yo’ll not
put upon us, my masters!’ And be danged to ’em, they shan’t this time!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A pivotal rebuttal where Nicholas directly challenges Margaret's southern assumptions, asserting northern working-class spirit and dignity against southern passivity and exploitation; a powerful class manifesto.
enrichment.best_quote: We just take our hands fro' our looms, and say, 'Yo' may clem us, but yo'll not put upon us, my masters!' And be danged to 'em, they shan't this time!
enrichment.summary: Nicholas defends the northern industrial workers as spirited and defiant, contrasting them with the oppressed, downtrodden labourers of the rural South.

text: “I wished I lived down South,” said Bessy.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's brief interjection reiterating her preference for the South, returning focus to her desire for escape.
enrichment.best_quote: I wished I lived down South,
enrichment.summary: Bessy reiterates her wish to live in the South.

text:
“There’s a deal to bear there,” said Margaret. “There are sorrows to
bear everywhere. There is very hard bodily labour to be gone through,
with very little food to give strength.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret begins to correct Bessy's romanticized view of the South by acknowledging rural hardship, complicating the north-south binary established earlier.
enrichment.best_quote: There are sorrows to bear everywhere. There is very hard bodily labour to be gone through, with very little food to give strength.
enrichment.summary: Margaret acknowledges that the South also suffers from poverty and hard labour without sufficient nourishment.

text:
“But it’s out of doors,” said Bessy. “And away from the endless, endless
noise, and sickening heat.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy counters with her specific complaint about industrial noise and heat, reinforcing her suffering and contrasting outdoor rural labour as preferable.
enrichment.best_quote: It's out of doors, and away from the endless, endless noise, and sickening heat.
enrichment.summary: Bessy counters that outdoor work, despite hardship, offers respite from the ceaseless noise and oppressive heat of the factory.

text:
“It’s sometimes in heavy rain, and sometimes in bitter cold. A young
person can stand it; but an old man gets racked with rheumatism, and
bent and withered before his time; yet he must just work on the same, or
else go to the workhouse.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret deepens her rebuttal with visceral detail about agricultural suffering—rain, cold, rheumatism, workhouse—presenting a grim southern reality that undermines Bessy's romanticization.
enrichment.best_quote: Yet he must just work on the same, or else go to the workhouse.
enrichment.summary: Margaret describes the brutal conditions of rural southern labour, including exposure to weather, physical deterioration, and the threat of the workhouse.

text: “I thought yo were so taken wi’ the ways of the South country.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas gently calls out Margaret's inconsistency, establishing a moment of friendly challenge.
enrichment.best_quote: I thought yo were so taken wi' the ways of the South country.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas playfully points out that Margaret has been praising the South while now describing its hardships.

text:
“So I am,” said Margaret, smiling a little, as she found herself thus
caught. “I only mean, Bessy, there’s good and bad in everything in this
world; and as you felt the bad up here, I thought it was but fair you
should know the bad down there.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret's response shows intellectual honesty and nuance; she acknowledges her earlier praise while clarifying that good and bad exist everywhere, avoiding simplistic regional comparison.
enrichment.best_quote: I only mean, Bessy, there's good and bad in everything in this world; and as you felt the bad up here, I thought it was but fair you should know the bad down there.
enrichment.summary: Margaret clarifies that she appreciates the South but acknowledges its hardships, arguing for balanced perspective rather than idealization.

text: “And yo say they never strike down there?” asked Nicholas abruptly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas abruptly pivots the conversation back to strikes, testing Margaret's knowledge and perhaps her judgment.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas suddenly asks whether southern workers strike, redirecting attention back to labour unrest.

text: “No!” said Margaret; “I think they have too much sense.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret dismisses southern strikes as unnecessary due to southern workers' good sense, but this proves naïve and provocative to Nicholas, triggering his ideological response.
enrichment.best_quote: I think they have too much sense.
enrichment.summary: Margaret asserts that southern workers do not strike because they are wise, implying strike action is foolish.

text:
“An’ I think,” replied he, dashing the ashes out of his pipe with so
much vehemence that it broke, “it’s not that they’ve too much sense, but
that they’ve too little spirit.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas's vehement rebuttal reframes Margaret's 'sense' as cowardice and lack of spirit; he equates strike action with self-respect and masculine dignity, offering a powerful working-class ideology.
enrichment.best_quote: An' I think it's not that they've too much sense, but that they've too little spirit.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas contends that southern workers lack not wisdom but courage and pride, attacking the notion that accepting low wages is sensible.

text:
“Oh, father!” said Bessy, “what have ye gained by striking? Just think
of that first strike when mother died—how we all had to clem—you the
worst of all; and yet many a one went in every week at the same wage,
till all were gone in that there was work for; and some went beggars all
their lives at after.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's painful recollection of a previous failed strike in which her mother died and the family starved reveals the human cost of labour action and directly contradicts her father's optimism.
enrichment.best_quote: Just think of that first strike when mother died—how we all had to clem—you the worst of all; and yet many a one went in every week at the same wage, till all were gone in that there was work for; and some went beggars all their lives at after.
enrichment.summary: Bessy reminds her father that during a previous strike her mother died and the family starved, while some workers defected anyway and later became permanent beggars.

text:
“Ay,” said he. “That there strike was badly managed. Folk got into th’
management of it, as were either fools or not true men. Yo’ll see, it’ll
be different this time.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas acknowledges past failure but dismisses it as due to incompetent leadership, asserting confidence in this strike's better management—revealing his persistent optimism despite trauma.
enrichment.best_quote: That there strike was badly managed. Folk got into th' management of it, as were either fools or not true men.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas dismisses the previous strike's failure as resulting from poor or dishonest leadership, promising better management this time.

text:
“But all this time you’ve not told me what you’re striking for,” said
Margaret, again.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret redirects to the central pedagogical question of the chapter, requesting a clear statement of strike demands.
enrichment.best_quote: But all this time you've not told me what you're striking for,
enrichment.summary: Margaret notes that despite the lengthy discussion, Nicholas has not clearly stated the strike's purpose.

text:
“Why, yo see, there’s five or six masters who have set themselves again
paying the wages they’ve been paying these two years past, and
flourishing upon, and getting richer upon. And now they come to us, and
say we’re to take less. And we won’t. We’ll just clem them to death
first; and see who’ll work for ’em then. They’ll have killed the goose
that laid ’em the golden eggs, I reckon.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas finally articulates the strike's cause: masters cutting wages despite past prosperity, with workers resolute to resist unto death rather than accept reduction. A key exposition of labour demands.
enrichment.best_quote: And now they come to us, and say we're to take less. And we won't. We'll just clem them to death first; and see who'll work for 'em then.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas explains that masters are demanding wage cuts despite years of profit, and workers refuse, determined to starve rather than yield.

text: “And so you plan dying, in order to be revenged upon them!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret misinterprets Nicholas's resistance as suicidal spite, prompting him to reframe strike action as noble sacrifice comparable to military duty.
enrichment.best_quote: And so you plan dying, in order to be revenged upon them!
enrichment.summary: Margaret accuses Nicholas of planning to starve to death out of spite against the masters.

text:
“No,” said he, “I dunnot. I just look forward to the chance of dying at
my post sooner than yield. That’s what folk call fine and honourable in
a soldier, and why not in a poor weaver-chap?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas reframes strike sacrifice as honourable duty, likening workers' willingness to die for justice to soldiers' patriotic deaths—a powerful assertion of working-class dignity and moral equivalence.
enrichment.best_quote: That's what folk call fine and honourable in a soldier, and why not in a poor weaver-chap?
enrichment.summary: Nicholas argues that if soldiers' willingness to die for their nation is honourable, why should workers' willingness to sacrifice for fair wages not be equally honourable?

text:
“But,” said Margaret, “a soldier dies in the cause of the Nation—in the
cause of others.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret counters that soldiers act for the nation rather than selfish revenge, establishing a key distinction between public and private motivation.
enrichment.best_quote: a soldier dies in the cause of the Nation—in the cause of others.
enrichment.summary: Margaret distinguishes between soldiers' sacrifice for the nation versus what she perceives as workers' self-interested revenge.

text:
He laughed grimly. “My lass,” said he, “yo’re but a young wench, but
don’t yo think I can keep three people—that’s Bessy, and Mary, and
me—on sixteen shillings a week? Dun yo think it’s for mysel’ I’m
striking work at this time? It is just as much in the cause of others as
yon soldier—only m’appen, the cause he dies for is just that of
somebody he never clapt eyes on, nor heerd on all his born days, while I
take up John Boucher’s cause, as lives next door but one, wi’ a sickly
wife, and eight childer, none on ’em factory age; and I don’t take up
his cause only, though he’s a poor good-for-nought, as can only manage
two looms at a time, but I take up th’ cause o’ justice. Why are we to
have less wage now, I ask, than two year ago?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A magnificent passage in which Nicholas articulates the strike as collective action for justice across the labouring community, not selfish vengeance. He names John Boucher, explains interdependence, and asserts workers' moral cause—one of the chapter's most significant statements.
enrichment.best_quote: I take up th' cause o' justice. Why are we to have less wage now, I ask, than two year ago?
enrichment.summary: Nicholas passionately argues that strikes are a moral and communal act of justice, exemplified by his support for John Boucher, and insists workers deserve fair compensation for their labour.

text:
“Don’t ask me,” said Margaret; “I am very ignorant. Ask some of your
masters. Surely they will give you a reason for it. It is not merely an
arbitrary decision of theirs, come to without reason.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret deflects, claiming ignorance and suggesting Nicholas consult the masters directly; a naive and somewhat evasive response.
enrichment.best_quote: Ask some of your masters. Surely they will give you a reason for it.
enrichment.summary: Margaret suggests that Nicholas ask the masters directly for their justification of wage cuts rather than pursuing a confrontational strike.

text:
“Yo’re just a foreigner, and nothing more,” said he, contemptuously.
“Much yo know about it. Ask th’ masters! They’d tell us to mind our own
business, and they’d mind theirs. Our business being, yo understand, to
take the bated wage, and be thankful; and their business to bate us down
to clemming point, to swell their profits. That’s what it is.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas dismisses Margaret as ignorant outsider while articulating the power dynamic and manipulation behind 'state of trade'—exposing the masters' rhetorical strategy and his class-conscious critique.
enrichment.best_quote: Our business being, yo understand, to take the bated wage, and be thankful; and their business to bate us down to clemming point, to swell their profits.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas contemptuously dismisses Margaret's suggestion and exposes what he sees as the cynical business relationship: workers starve to enrich masters.

text:
“But,” said Margaret, determined not to give way, although she saw she
was irritating him, “the state of trade may be such as not to enable
them to give you the same remuneration.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret persists with a sophisticated economic argument about trade conditions, attempting to rescue objectivity from Nicholas's passionate critique.
enrichment.summary: Margaret argues that trade conditions may genuinely prevent masters from maintaining wages rather than operating from pure greed.

text:
“State o’ trade! That’s just a piece o’ masters’ humbug. It’s rate o’
wages I was talking of. Th’ masters keep th’ state o’ trade in their own
hands; and just walk it forward like a black bug-a-boo, to frighten
naughty children with into being good. I’ll tell you it’s their
part,—their cue, as some folks call it,—to beat us down, to swell
their fortunes; and it’s ours to stand up and fight hard,—not for
ourselves alone, but for them round about us—for justice and fair play.
We help to make their profits, and we ought to help spend ’em. It’s not
that we want their brass so much this time, as we’ve done many a time
afore. We’n getten money laid by; and we’re resolved to stand and fall
together; not a man on us will go in for less wage than th’ Union says
is our due. So I say, ‘hooray for the strike,’ and let Thornton, and
Slickson, and Hamper, and their set look to it!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas's most comprehensive rebuttal, denouncing 'state of trade' as a scare tactic, reasserting workers' moral claim to share masters' profits, invoking Union solidarity, and naming the specific masters—a brilliant synthesis of his political argument.
enrichment.best_quote: We help to make their profits, and we ought to help spend 'em.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas systematically refutes 'state of trade' as masters' manipulation, asserts workers' collective right to fair profit-sharing, invokes Union solidarity and fixed wage demands, and names the specific masters they oppose.

text: “Thornton!” said Margaret. “Mr. Thornton of Marlborough Street?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret's sudden focus on John Thornton signals a shift in her emotional engagement; naming him here connects the strike abstraction to a concrete figure of romantic and ideological significance.
enrichment.summary: Margaret expresses surprise and concern that John Thornton is one of the masters in the strike dispute.

text: “Aye! Thornton o’ Marlborough Mill, as we call him.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas confirms Thornton's status as a target master, establishing his position within the labour conflict.
enrichment.best_quote: Thornton o' Marlborough Mill, as we call him.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas confirms that John Thornton of Marlborough Mill is indeed one of the masters against whom the strike is directed.

text:
“He is one of the masters you are striving with, is he not? What sort of
a master is he?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret requests characterization of Thornton as a master, with personal interest evident beneath the surface inquiry.
enrichment.summary: Margaret asks Nicholas to describe what kind of master John Thornton is.

text:
“Did yo’ ever see a bulldog? Set a bulldog on hind legs, and dress him
up in coat and breeches, and yo’n just getten John Thornton.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas's witty comparison of Thornton to a bulldog establishes a signature image; crude but memorable, setting up Margaret's gentle correction and following character portraits.
enrichment.best_quote: Did yo' ever see a bulldog? Set a bulldog on hind legs, and dress him up in coat and breeches, and yo'n just getten John Thornton.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas humorously compares Thornton to a bulldog dressed in human clothing, suggesting his obstinate, brutish nature.

text:
“Nay,” said Margaret, laughing, “I deny that. Mr. Thornton is plain
enough, but he’s not like a bulldog, with its short broad nose, and
snarling upper lip.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret gently defends Thornton's appearance, establishing her personal investment in his character and dignity, with playful tone indicating affection.
enrichment.best_quote: Mr. Thornton is plain enough, but he's not like a bulldog, with its short broad nose, and snarling upper lip.
enrichment.summary: Margaret playfully defends Thornton, acknowledging his plain appearance while denying the bulldog comparison.

text:
“No! not in look, I grant yo. But let John Thornton get hold on a
notion, and he’ll stick to it like a bulldog; yo might pull him away wi’
a pitchfork ere he’d leave go. He’s worth fighting wi’, is John
Thornton. As for Slickson, I take it, some o’ these days he’ll wheedle
his men back wi’ fair promises; that they’ll just get cheated out of as
soon as they’re in his power again. He’ll work his fines well out on
’em, I’ll warrant. He’s as slippery as an eel, he is. He’s like a
cat,—as sleek, and cunning, and fierce. It’ll never be an honest up and
down fight wi’ him, as it will be wi’ Thornton. Thornton’s as dour as a
door-nail; an obstinate chap, every inch on him,—th’ oud bulldog!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas's extended character portraits of Thornton, Slickson, and Hamper reveal workers' keen reading of employers' personalities and strategies; Thornton emerges as principled but obstinate, worthy of respect-as-opponent.
enrichment.best_quote: Let John Thornton get hold on a notion, and he'll stick to it like a bulldog; yo might pull him away wi' a pitchfork ere he'd leave go. He's worth fighting wi', is John Thornton.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas elaborates his characterizations: Thornton is principled and stubborn, a worthy adversary; Slickson is deceptive and cunning; Hamper is unspecified but included among masters to oppose.

text:
“Poor Bessy!” said Margaret, turning round to her. “You sigh over it
all. You don’t like struggling and fighting as your father does, do
you?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret redirects to Bessy's emotional state, showing concern and empathy, preparing for the emotional turn toward Bessy's confession and health anxiety.
enrichment.best_quote: You sigh over it all. You don't like struggling and fighting as your father does, do you?
enrichment.summary: Margaret expresses compassion for Bessy's visible distress about the strike and family conflict.

text:
“No!” said she, heavily. “I’m sick on it. I could have wished to have
had other talk about me in my latter days, than just the clashing and
clanging and clattering that has ever wearied a’ my life long, about
work and wages, and masters, and hands, and knobsticks.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's confession reveals both her physical and emotional exhaustion from a lifetime of labour-related noise, conflict, and tension; a poignant statement of weariness and desire for peace.
enrichment.best_quote: I'm sick on it. I could have wished to have had other talk about me in my latter days, than just the clashing and clanging and clattering that has ever wearied a' my life long, about work and wages, and masters, and hands, and knobsticks.
enrichment.summary: Bessy expresses exhaustion with strikes and labour dispute discourse, yearning for peace and quiet in what she senses are her final days.

text:
“Poor wench! latter days be farred! Thou’rt looking a sight better
already for a little stir and change. Beside, I shall be a deal here to
make it more lively for thee.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas reassures Bessy, insisting she is improving and promising to keep her company, revealing paternal tenderness amid labour conflicts.
enrichment.best_quote: Thou'rt looking a sight better already for a little stir and change.
enrichment.summary: Nicholas tries to cheer Bessy, claiming she looks healthier and promising to spend more time at home.

text: “Tobacco-smoke chokes me!” said she, querulously.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy complains of tobacco smoke, leading Nicholas to make a tender gesture, though Bessy's subsequent comments hint at her knowledge that he will smoke elsewhere.
enrichment.summary: Bessy complains that tobacco smoke makes her ill.

text:
“Then I’ll never smoke no more i’ the house!” he replied, tenderly. “But
why didst thou not tell me afore, thou foolish wench?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nicholas's tender response, offering to quit smoking indoors, shows his love for Bessy and willingness to sacrifice for her comfort.
enrichment.best_quote: Then I'll never smoke no more i' the house!
enrichment.summary: Nicholas immediately promises to stop smoking indoors out of concern for Bessy's health.

text:
She did not speak for a while, and then so low that only Margaret heard
her:

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief narrative transition noting Bessy's silence and her barely audible comment heard only by Margaret; suggests intimacy and impending revelation.
enrichment.summary: Bessy falls silent, then whispers something so quietly that only Margaret hears.

text:
“I reckon, he’ll want a’ the comfort he can get out o’ either pipe or
drink afore he’s done.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's ominous whisper—that Nicholas will seek solace in pipe or drink during the strike—reveals her deep knowledge of his character and her fear of the strike's psychological toll on him.
enrichment.best_quote: I reckon, he'll want a' the comfort he can get out o' either pipe or drink afore he's done.

“No—not to say drink,” replied she, still in the same wild excited
tone. “But what win ye have? There are days wi’ you as wi’ other folk, I
suppose, when yo’ get up and go through th’ hours, just longing for a
bit of a change—a bit of a fillip, as it were. I know I ha’ gone and
bought a four-pounder out o’ another baker’s shop to common on such
days, just because I sickened at the thought of going on for ever wi’
the same sight in my eyes, and the same sound in my ears, and the same
taste i’ my mouth, and the same thought (or no thought, for that matter)
in my head, day after day, for ever. I’ve longed for to be a man to go
spreeing, even if it were only a tramp to some new place in search o’
work. And father—all men—have it stronger in ’em than me to get tired
o’ sameness and work for ever. And what is ’em to do? It’s little blame
to them if they do go into th’ gin-shop for to make their blood flow
quicker, and more lively, and see things they never see at no other
time—pictures, and looking-glass, and such like. But father never was a
drunkard, though maybe, he’s got worse for drink, now and then. Only yo’
see,” and now her voice took a mournful, pleading tone, “at times o’
strike there’s much to knock a man down, for all they start so
hopefully; and where’s the comfort to come fro’? He’ll get angry and
mad—they all do—and then they get tired out wi’ being angry and mad,
and maybe ha’ done things in their passion they’d be glad to forget.
Bless yo’r sweet pitiful face! but yo’ dunnot know what a strike is
yet.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A remarkable passage in which Bessy articulates the psychological and social pressures on working-class men during strikes: the need for escape from monotony, the attractions of gin-shops as sensory escape, and the cycle of passion and violence that strikes produce. Culminates with her sobering judgment that Margaret does not yet understand strikes.
enrichment.best_quote: Bless yo'r sweet pitiful face! but yo' dunnot know what a strike is yet.
enrichment.summary: Bessy explains that men drink not from addiction but from the psychological need for relief from endless monotony and routine; during strikes, this impulse intensifies amid the emotional turbulence and risk of violence.

“Take care,” said Margaret, her cheek flushing, and her eye lightening,
“how you judge, Bessy. I shall go home to my mother, who is so ill—so
ill, Bessy, that there’s no outlet but death for her out of prison of
her great suffering; and yet I must speak cheerfully to my father, who
has no notion of her real state, and to whom the knowledge must come
gradually. The only person—the only one who could sympathise with me
and help me—whose presence could comfort my mother more than any other
earthly thing—is falsely accused—would run the risk of death if he
came to see his dying mother. This I tell you—only you, Bessy. You must
not mention it. No other person in Milton—hardly any other person in
England knows. Have I not care? Do I not know anxiety, though I go about
well-dressed, and have food enough? Oh, Bessy, God is just, and our lots
are well portioned out by Him, although none but He knows the bitterness
of our souls.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret's powerful rebuttal reveals her own hidden suffering: her mother's terminal illness, her father's ignorance, and Frederick's danger as a fugitive. She confides only in Bessy, asserting God's justice and the complexity of hidden grief beneath respectable appearance. A pivotal character moment.

enrichment.summary: Margaret reveals her hidden griefs to Bessy: her mother's imminent death, her father's ignorance, and her brother Frederick's danger as a fugitive from justice—asserting that privilege does not protect from suffering.

“I ask your pardon,” replied Bessy, humbly. “Sometimes, when I’ve
thought o’ my life, and the little pleasure I’ve had in it, I’ve
believed that, maybe, I was one of those doomed to die by the falling of
a star from heaven; ‘And the name of the star is called Wormwood; and
the third part of the waters became wormwood; and men died of the
waters, because they were made bitter.’ One can bear pain and sorrow
better if one thinks it has been prophesied long before for one:
somehow, then it seems as if my pain was needed for the fulfilment;
otherways it seems all sent for nothing.”

enrichment.summary: Bessy apologizes and confesses her fatalism: she has believed her suffering was prophesied by scripture (Revelation's Wormwood), giving it cosmic meaning rather than senseless randomness.

annoying thought. Fanny asked her mother numerous small questions, all
having nothing to do with the subject, which a wiser person would have
perceived was occupying her attention. Consequently, she received many
short answers. She was not sorry when, at ten o’clock, the servants
filed in to prayers. These her mother always read,—first reading a
chapter. They were now working steadily through the Old Testament. When
prayers were ended, and his mother had wished him good-night, with that
long steady look of hers which conveyed no expression of the tenderness
that was in her heart, but yet had the intensity of a blessing, Mr.
Thornton continued his walk. All his business plans had received a
check, a sudden pull-up, from this approaching turn-out. The forethought

folly, which would injure themselves even more than him, though no one
could set any limit to the mischief they were doing. And these were the

of their capital; Hamper had said, only this very day, that if he were
ruined by the strike, he would start life again, comforted by the
conviction that those who had brought it on were in a worse predicament

hands; and if they drove away their market, they could not follow it,

text:
They needed this gleam of brightness in-doors, for out-of-doors, even to
their uninstructed eyes, there was a gloomy brooding appearance of
discontent. Mr. Hale had his own acquaintances among the working men,
and was depressed with their earnestly-told tales of suffering and
long-endurance. They would have scorned to speak of what they had to
bear to any one who might, from his position, have understood it without
their words. But here was this man, from a distant county, who was
perplexed by the workings of a system into the midst of which he was
thrown, and each was eager to make him a judge, and to bring witness of
his own causes for irritation. Then Mr. Hale brought all his budget of
grievances, and laid it before Mr. Thornton, for him, with his
experience as a master, to arrange them, and explain their origin; which
he always did, on sound economical principles; showing that, as trade
was conducted, there must always be a waxing and waning of commercial
prosperity; and that in the waning a certain number of masters, as well
as of men, must go down into ruin, and be no more seen among the ranks
of the happy and prosperous. He spoke as if this consequence were so
entirely logical, that neither employers nor employed had any right to
complain if it became their fate: the employer to turn aside from the
race he could no longer run, with a bitter sense of incompetency and
failure—wounded in the struggle—trampled down by his fellows in their
haste to get rich—slighted where he was once honoured—humbly asking
for, instead of bestowing, employment with a lordly hand. Of course,
speaking so of the fate that, as a master, might be his own in the
fluctuations of commerce, he was not likely to have more sympathy with
that of the workmen, who were passed by in the swift merciless
improvement or alteration; who would fain lie down and quietly die out
of the world that needed them not, but felt as they could never rest in
their graves for the clinging cries of the beloved and helpless they
would leave behind; who envied the power of the wild bird, that can feed
her young with her very heart’s blood. Margaret’s whole soul rose up
against him while he reasoned in this way—as if commerce were
everything and humanity nothing. She could hardly thank him for the
individual kindness, which brought him that very evening to offer
her—for the delicacy which made him understand that he must offer her
privately—every convenience for illness that his own wealth or his
mother’s foresight had caused them to accumulate in their household, and
which, as he learnt from Dr. Donaldson, Mrs. Hale might possibly
require. His presence, after the way he had spoken—his bringing before
her the doom, which she was vainly trying to persuade herself might yet
be averted from her mother—all conspired to set Margaret’s teeth on
edge, as she looked at him, and listened to him. What business had he to
be the only person, except Dr. Donaldson and Dixon, admitted to the
awful secret, which she held shut up in the most dark and sacred recess
of her heart—not daring to look at it, unless she invoked heavenly
strength to bear the sight—that, some day soon, she should cry aloud
for her mother, and no answer would come out of the blank, dumb
darkness? Yet he knew all. She saw it in his pitying eyes. She heard it
in his grave and tremulous voice. How reconcile those eyes, that voice,
with the hard, reasoning, dry, merciless way in which he laid down
axioms of trade, and serenely followed them out to their full
consequences? The discord jarred upon her inexpressibly. The more
because of the gathering woe of which she heard from Bessy. To be sure,
Nicholas Higgins, the father, spoke differently. He had been appointed a
committee-man, and said that he knew secrets of which the exoteric knew
nothing. He said this more expressly and particularly, on the very day
before Mrs. Thornton’s dinner-party. When Margaret, going in to speak to
Bessy, found him arguing the point with Boucher, the neighbour of whom
she had frequently heard mention, as by turns exciting Higgins’s
compassion, as an unskilful workman with a large family depending upon
him for support, and at other times enraging his more energetic and
sanguine neighbour by his want of what the latter called spirit. It was
very evident that Higgins was in a passion when Margaret entered.
Boucher stood, with both hands on the rather high mantelpiece, swaying
himself a little on the support which his arms, thus placed, gave him,
and looking wildly into the fire, with a kind of despair that irritated
Higgins, even while it went to his heart. Bessy was rocking herself
violently backwards and forwards, as was her wont (Margaret knew by this
time) when she was agitated. Her sister Mary was tying on her bonnet (in
great clumsy bows, as suited her great clumsy fingers), to go to her
fustian-cutting, blubbering out loud the while, and evidently longing to
be away from a scene that distressed her.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Masterful extended exposition on industrial unrest and Thornton's economic philosophy. Shows the clash between humanistic compassion and cold commercial logic; deeply thematic and revealing of both Thornton's character and Margaret's moral conflict.
enrichment.best_quote: He spoke as if this consequence were so entirely logical, that neither employers nor employed had any right to complain if it became their fate: the employer to turn aside from the race he could no longer run, with a bitter sense of incompetency and failure—wounded in the struggle—trampled down by his fellows in their haste to get rich—slighted where he was once honoured—humbly asking for, instead of bestowing, employment with a lordly hand.
enrichment.summary: The household witnesses growing discontent among workers. Mr. Hale hears workers' grievances and brings them to Thornton, who explains industrial fluctuation with cold economic principles, showing no sympathy for either masters or workers facing ruin. Margaret is appalled by his reasoning and troubled by his knowledge of her mother's illness.

Margaret came in upon this scene. She stood for a moment at the
door—then, her finger on her lips, she stole to a seat on the squab
near Bessy. Nicholas saw her come in, and greeted her with a gruff, but
not unfriendly nod. Mary hurried out of the house, catching gladly at
the open door, and crying aloud when she got away from her father’s
presence. It was only John Boucher that took no notice whatever who came
in and who went out.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid dramatic scene showing the Higgins household in turmoil—Boucher's despair, Bessy's agitation, Mary's distress. Atomspheric and emotionally charged, demonstrating the human cost of the strike.
enrichment.summary: Margaret arrives at the Higgins household to find an intense scene: Higgins arguing passionately while Boucher stands in despair by the mantel; Bessy rocks agitatedly; Mary hurries out, upset.

text:
“It’s no use, Higgins. Hoo cannot live long a’ this’n. Hoo’s just
sinking away—not for want o’ meat hersel’—but because hoo cannot stand
th’ sight o’ the little ones clemming. Ay, clemming! Five shilling a
week may do well enough for thee, wi’ but two mouths to fill, and one on
’em a wench who can well earn her own meat. But it’s clemming to us. An’
I tell thee plain—if hoo dies, as I’m ’feard hoo will afore we’ve
getten th’ five per cent., I’ll fling the money back i’ th’ master’s
face, and say, ‘Be domned to yo’; be domned to th’ whole cruel world o’
yo’; that could na leave me th’ best wife that ever bore childer to a
man. An’ look thee lad, I’ll hate thee, and th’ whole pack o’ th’ Union.
Ay, an’ chase yo’ through heaven wi’ my hatred,—I will, lad! I
will,—if yo’re leading me astray i’ this matter. Thou saidst, Nicholas,
on Wednesday sennight—and it’s now Tuesday i’ th’ second week—that
afore a fortnight we’d ha’ the masters coming a-begging to us to take
back our work, at our own wage—and time’s nearly up,—and there’s our
lile Jack lying a-bed, too weak to cry, but just every now and then
sobbing up his heart for want o’ food,—our lile Jack, I tell thee, lad!
Hoo’s never looked up sin’ he were born, and hoo loves him as if he were
her very life,—as he is,—for I reckon he’ll ha’ cost me that precious
price,—our lile Jack, who wakened me each morn wi’ putting his sweet
little lips to my great rough fou’ face, a-seeking a smooth place to
kiss,—an’ he lies clemming.” Here the deep sobs choked the poor man and
Nicholas looked up, with eyes brimful of tears, to Margaret, before he
could gain courage to speak.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Boucher's heart-breaking speech about his wife's dying from watching the children starve is extraordinarily moving and poignant. The detail of little Jack's lips seeking a place to kiss his face is unbearably tender. This is unmissable dramatic and emotional material—a masterpiece of social pathos.
enrichment.best_quote: Our lile Jack, who wakened me each morn wi' putting his sweet little lips to my great rough fou' face, a-seeking a smooth place to kiss,—an' he lies clemming.
enrichment.summary: Boucher desperately tells Higgins that his wife is dying from watching their starving children; he accuses Higgins of misleading the men with false promises, and describes his son Jack's suffering with anguished tenderness.

text:
“Hou’d up, man. Thy lile Jack shall na’ clem. I ha’ gotten brass, and
we’ll go buy the chap a sup o’ milk an’ a good four-pounder this very
minute. What’s mine’s thine, sure enough, i’ thou’st i’ want. Only,
dunnot lose heart, man!” continued he, as he fumbled in a tea-pot for
what money he had. “I lay yo my heart and soul we’ll win for a’ this:
it’s but bearing on one more week, and yo’ just see th’ way th’ masters
’ll come round, praying on us to come back to our mills. An’ the
Union—that’s to say, I—will take care yo’ve enough for th’ childer and
th’ missus. So dunnot turn faint-heart, and go to th’ tyrants a-seeking
work.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Higgins's compassionate response—offering his own money and steadfast faith in the Union—shows his character. Complicated portrait of working-class solidarity and moral commitment.
enrichment.best_quote: Thy lile Jack shall na' clem. I ha' gotten brass, and we'll go buy the chap a sup o' milk an' a good four-pounder this very minute. What's mine's thine, sure enough, i' thou'st i' want.
enrichment.summary: Higgins offers Boucher money from his own pocket to buy milk and food for the child, insisting the Union will prevail within the week and promising to ensure Boucher's family does not go hungry.

text:
The man turned round at these words,—turned round a face so white, and
gaunt, and tear-furrowed, and hopeless, that its very calm forced
Margaret to weep.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Boucher's transformation to hopelessness is vividly portrayed; his gaunt face moves Margaret to tears and shows the terrible cost of the strike.
enrichment.summary: Boucher turns to face them, his expression so white, gaunt, and tear-worn that Margaret is moved to weep.

text:
“Yo’ know well, that a worser tyrant than e’er th’ masters were says,
‘Clem to death, and see ’em a’ clem to death, ere yo’ dare go again th’
Union.’ Yo’ know it well, Nicholas, for a’ yo’re one on e’m. Yo’ may be
kind hearts, each separate; but once banded together, yo’ve no more pity
for a man than a wild hunger-maddened wolf.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Boucher's bitter indictment of the Union as a merciless tyranny is powerful and polemical. Shows the moral complexity of collective action and the cost of solidarity to individuals in desperation.
enrichment.best_quote: Yo' know well, that a worser tyrant than e'er th' masters were says, 'Clem to death, and see 'em a' clem to death, ere yo' dare go again th' Union.' Yo' know it well, Nicholas, for a' yo're one on e'm. Yo' may be kind hearts, each separate; but once banded together, yo've no more pity for a man than a wild hunger-maddened wolf.
enrichment.summary: Boucher accuses Higgins and the Union of tyranny—forcing men to starve rather than break ranks, and showing no individual compassion when united.

text:
Nicholas had his hand on the lock of the door—he stopped and turned
round on Boucher, close following:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Action beat showing Higgins stopping at the door; minimal narrative significance.
enrichment.summary: Higgins stops at the door, turning to respond to Boucher's accusation.

“So help me God! man alive—if I think not I’m doing best for thee, and
for all on us. If I’m going wrong when I think I’m going right, it’s
their sin, who ha’ left me where I am, in my ignorance. I ha’ thought
till my brains ached,—Beli’ me, John, I have. An’ I say again, there’s
no help for us but having faith i’ th’ Union. They’ll win the day, see
if they dunnot!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Higgins's earnest defense of his convictions shows his integrity and internal conflict. Philosophical and emotionally resonant statement of his faith in the Union.
enrichment.best_quote: So help me God! man alive—if I think not I'm doing best for thee, and for all on us. If I'm going wrong when I think I'm going right, it's their sin, who ha' left me where I am, in my ignorance.
enrichment.summary: Higgins insists he believes in his course and calls God to witness his conviction that the Union is the workers' only hope.

Not one word had Margaret or Bessy spoken. They had hardly uttered the
sighing, that the eyes of each called to the other to bring up from the
depths of her heart. At last Bessy said,

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret and Bessy's silent response shows their emotional reaction; marks transition to Bessy's response.
enrichment.summary: Margaret and Bessy remain silent, their eyes communicating their deep distress at the exchange.

“I never thought to hear father call on God again. But yo’ heard him
say, ‘So help me God!’”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's observation about her father's invocation of God suggests spiritual transformation; minor moment of character insight.
enrichment.summary: Bessy notes that her father invoked God's name, something she had never heard him do before.

“Yes!” said Margaret. “Let me bring you what money I can spare,—let me
bring you a little food for that poor man’s children. Don’t let them
know it comes from any one but your father. It will be but little.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret's offer of money and food to help Boucher's children shows her immediate compassionate response and personal sacrifice, demonstrating her Christian values in action.
enrichment.summary: Margaret offers Bessy what money she can spare and asks her to provide food for Boucher's children secretly, as if from their father.

text:
Bessy lay back without taking any notice of what Margaret said. She did
not cry—she only quivered up her breath.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's emotional reaction—quivering breath without tears—shows her exhaustion and emotional depletion.
enrichment.summary: Bessy does not respond to Margaret's offer but sits back, her breath quivering, too drained for tears.

text:
“My heart’s drained dry o’ tears,” she said. “Boucher’s been in these
days past, a telling me of his fears and his troubles. He’s but a weak
kind of chap, I know, but he’s a man for a’ that; and tho’ I’ve been
angry, many a time afore now, wi’ him an’ his wife, as knew no more nor
him how to manage, yet yo’ see, all folks isn’t wise, yet God lets ’em
live—ay, an’ gives ’em some one to love, and be loved by, just as good
as Solomon. An’ if sorrow comes to them they love, it hurts ’em as sore
as e’er it did Solomon. I can’t make it out. Perhaps it’s as well such a
one as Boucher has th’ Union to see after him. But I’d just like for to
see th’ men as make th’ Union, and put ’em one by one face to face wi’
Boucher. I reckon, if they heard him, the’d tell him (if I cotched ’em
one by one), he might go back and get what he could for his work, even
if it weren’t so much as they ordered.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's meditation on suffering, on God's love for all regardless of wisdom, and her call for Union leaders to face individual workers like Boucher is profound and touching. Shows Bessy's moral wisdom and compassion despite her illness.
enrichment.best_quote: Perhaps it's as well such a one as Boucher has th' Union to see after him. But I'd just like for to see th' men as make th' Union, and put 'em one by one face to face wi' Boucher. I reckon, if they heard him, the'd tell him (if I cotched 'em one by one), he might go back and get what he could for his work, even if it weren't so much as they ordered.
enrichment.summary: Bessy reflects on Boucher's weakness and sorrow, notes that God loves all people equally, and expresses the wish that Union leaders would face Boucher individually—suggesting they might show mercy if they heard his story.

text:
Margaret sat utterly silent. How was she ever to go away into comfort
and forget that man’s voice, with the tone of unutterable agony, telling
more by far than his words of what he had to suffer? She took out her
purse; she had not much in it of what she could call her own, but what
she had she put into Bessy’s hands without speaking.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Margaret's silence and emotional response (opening her purse despite limited means) shows her being deeply moved and compelled to act morally despite her own constraints.
enrichment.summary: Margaret is silenced by the weight of Boucher's suffering and gives Bessy her own limited money without speaking.

text:
“Thank yo’. There’s many on ’em gets no more, and is not so bad
off,—leastways does not show it as he does. But father won’t let ’em
want, now he knows. Yo’ see, Boucher’s been pulled down wi’ his
childer,—and her being so cranky, and a’ they could pawn has gone this
last twelvemonth. Yo’re not to think we’d ha’ letten ’em clem, for all
we’re a bit pressed oursel’; if neighbours doesn’t see after neighbours,
I dunno who will.” Bessy seemed almost afraid lest Margaret should think
they had not the will, and, to a certain degree, the power of helping
one whom she evidently regarded as having a claim upon them. “Besides,”
she went on, “father is sure and positive the masters must give in
within these next few days,—that they canna hould on much longer. But I
thank yo’ all the same,—I thank yo’ for mysel’, as much as for Boucher,
for it jus makes my heart warm to yo’ more and more.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's explanation and assurance that the community will help—despite their own hardship—shows working-class solidarity and mutual care. Demonstrates the human connections beneath industrial conflict.
enrichment.summary: Bessy thanks Margaret and explains that Boucher's family, though pressed, will be supported by neighbors and especially by her father now that he knows their need.

text:
Bessy seemed much quieter to-day, but fearfully languid and exhausted.
As she finished speaking, she looked so faint and weary that Margaret
became alarmed.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Description of Bessy's declining health; shows the toll of emotional turmoil on her fragile condition.
enrichment.summary: Bessy appears increasingly languid and exhausted; Margaret becomes alarmed at her faint, weary appearance.

text:
“It’s nout,” said Bessy. “It’s not death yet. I had a fearfu’ night wi’
dreams—or somewhat like dreams, for I were wide awake—and I’m all in a
swounding daze to-day,—only yon poor chap made me alive again. No! it’s
not death yet, but death is not far off. Ay. Cover me up, and I’ll may
be sleep, if th’ cough will let me. Good night—good afternoon, m’appen
I should say—but th’ light is dim an’ misty to-day.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bessy's poignant meditation on her approaching death, her sleepless feverish night, and her diminished will to live is deeply moving. Shows her acceptance and resignation. Thematically powerful.

enrichment.summary: Bessy acknowledges her approaching death, describes her restless fevered night, and expresses her confused, weakened state as the light dims into mist.

“By the soft green light in the woody glade, 
 On the banks of moss where thy childhood played 
 By the household tree, thro’ which thine eye 
 First looked in love to the summer sky.”

text:
Margaret  was once more in her morning dress, travelling quietly home
with her father, who had come up to assist at the wedding. Her mother
had been detained at home by a multitude of half-reasons, none of which
anybody fully understood, except Mr. Hale, who was perfectly aware that
all his arguments in favour of a grey satin gown, which was midway
between oldness and newness, had proved unavailing; and that, as he had
not the money to equip his wife afresh, from top to toe, she would not
show herself at her only sister’s only child’s wedding. If Mrs. Shaw had
guessed at the real reason why Mrs. Hale did not accompany her husband,
she would have showered down gowns upon her; but it was nearly twenty
years since Mrs. Shaw had been the poor pretty Miss Beresford, and she
had really forgotten all grievances except that of the unhappiness
arising from disparity of age in married life, on which she could
descant by the half-hour. Dearest Maria had married the man of her
heart, only eight years older than herself, with the sweetest temper,
and that blue black hair one so seldom sees. Mr. Hale was one of the
most delightful preachers she had ever heard, and a perfect model of a
parish priest. Perhaps it was not quite a logical deduction from all
these premises, but it was still Mrs. Shaw’s characteristic conclusion,
as she thought over her sister’s lot: “Married for love, what can
dearest Maria have to wish for in this world?” Mrs. Hale, if she spoke
truth, might have answered with a ready-made list, “a silver-grey glacé
silk, a white chip bonnet, oh! dozens of things for the wedding, and
hundreds of things for the house.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes Margaret's return home and introduces family dynamics, with some social commentary on gentility and financial constraint.
enrichment.best_quote: Married for love, what can dearest Maria have to wish for in this world?
enrichment.summary: Margaret returns home from a wedding with her father; her mother remained behind due to financial constraints, unaware of which Mrs. Shaw would have remedied with gifts.

text:
Margaret only knew that her mother had not found it convenient to come,
and she was not sorry to think that their meeting and greeting would
take place at Helstone parsonage, rather than, during the confusion of
the last two or three days, in the house in Harley Street, where she
herself had had to play the part of Figaro, and was wanted everywhere at
one and the same time. Her mind and body ached now with the recollection
of all she had done and said within the last forty-eight hours. The
farewells so hurriedly taken, amongst all the other good-byes, of those
she had lived with so long, oppressed her now with a sad regret for the
times that were no more; it did not signify what those times had been,
they were gone never to return. Margaret’s heart felt more heavy than
she could ever have thought it possible in going to her own dear home,
the place and the life she had longed for for years—at that time of all
times for yearning and longing, just before the sharp senses lose their
outlines in sleep. She took her mind away with a wrench from the
recollection of the past to the bright serene contemplation of the
hopeful future. Her eyes began to see, not visions of what had been, but
the sight actually before her; her dear father leaning back asleep in
the railway carriage. His blue-black hair was grey now, and lay thinly
over his brows. The bones of his face were plainly to be seen—too
plainly for beauty, if his features had been less finely cut; as it was,
they had a grace if not a comeliness of their own. The face was in
repose; but it was rather rest after weariness than the serene calm of
the countenance of one who led a placid, contented life. Margaret was
painfully struck by the worn, anxious expression; and she went back over
the open and avowed circumstances of her father’s life, to find the
cause for the lines that spoke so plainly of habitual distress and
depression.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Margaret's emotional complexity and her perception of her father's distress, establishing key relational tensions and foreshadowing concern about Frederick.
enrichment.best_quote: The farewells so hurriedly taken, amongst all the other good-byes, of those she had lived with so long, oppressed her now with a sad regret for the times that were no more
enrichment.summary: Margaret observes her father's worn and anxious face on the journey home and worries about the unknown troubles burdening him.

“Poor Frederick!” thought she, sighing. “Oh! if Frederick had but been a
clergyman, instead of going into the navy, and being lost to us all! I
wish I knew all about it. I never understood it from Aunt Shaw; I only
knew he could not come back to England because of that terrible affair.
Poor dear papa! how sad he looks! I am so glad I am going home, to be at
hand to comfort him and mamma.”

She was ready with a bright smile, in which there was not a trace of
fatigue, to greet her father when he awakened. He smiled back again, but
faintly, as if it were an unusual exertion. His face returned into its
lines of habitual anxiety. He had a trick of half-opening his mouth as
if to speak, which constantly unsettled the form of the lips, and gave
the face an undecided expression. But he had the same large, soft eyes
as his daughter,—eyes which moved slowly and almost grandly round in
their orbits, and were well veiled by their transparent white eyelids.
Margaret was more like him than like her mother. Sometimes people
wondered that parents so handsome should have a daughter who was so far
regularly beautiful; not beautiful at all, was occasionally said. Her
mouth was wide; no rosebud that could only open just enough to let out a
“yes” and “no,” and “an’t please you, sir.” But the wide mouth was one
soft curve of rich red lips; and the skin, if not white and fair, was of
an ivory smoothness and delicacy. If the look on her face was, in
general, too dignified and reserved for one so young, now, talking to
her father, it was bright as the morning,—full of dimples, and glances
that spoke of childish gladness, and boundless hope in the future.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Contains detailed physical description of Margaret and her father, revealing character through appearance and establishing Margaret's vivid transformation when engaged.

enrichment.summary: Margaret and her father exchange smiles; the narrator describes their physical features and notes Margaret's uncommon beauty and capacity for brightness.

text:
It was the latter part of July when Margaret returned home. The forest
trees were all one dark, full, dusky green; the fern below them caught
all the slanting sunbeams; the weather was sultry and broodingly still.
Margaret used to tramp along by her father’s side, crushing down the
fern with a cruel glee, as she felt it yield under her light foot, and
send up the fragrance peculiar to it—out on the broad commons into the
warm scented light, seeing multitudes of wild, free, living creatures,
revelling in the sunshine, and the herbs and flowers it called forth.
This life—at least these walks—realised all Margaret’s anticipations.
She took a pride in her forest. Its people were her people. She made
hearty friends with them; learned and delighted in using their peculiar
words; took up her freedom amongst them; nursed their babies; talked or
read with slow distinctness to their old people; carried dainty messes
to their sick; resolved before long to teach at the school where her
father went regularly every day as to an appointed task, but she was
continually tempted off to go and see some individual friend—man,
woman, or child—in some cottage in the green shade of the forest. Her
out-of-doors life was perfect. Her in-doors life had its drawbacks. With
the healthy shame of a child, she blamed herself for her keenness of
sight in perceiving that all was not as it should be there. Her
mother—her mother always so kind and tender towards her—seemed now and
then so much discontented with their situation; thought that the bishop
strangely neglected his episcopal duties, in not giving Mr. Hale a
better living; and almost reproached her husband because he could not
bring himself to say that he wished to leave the parish, and undertake
the charge of a larger. He would sigh aloud as he answered, that if he
could do what he ought in little Helstone, he should be thankful; but
every day he was more overpowered; the world became more bewildering. At
each repeated urgency of his wife, that he would put himself in the way
of seeking some preferment, Margaret saw that her father shrank more and
more; and she strove at such times to reconcile her mother to Helstone.
Mrs. Hale said that the near neighbourhood of so many trees affected her
health; and Margaret would try to tempt her forth on to the beautiful,
broad, upland, sun-streaked, cloud-shadowed common; for she was sure
that her mother had accustomed herself too much to an in-doors life,
seldom extending her walks beyond the church, the school, and the
neighbouring cottages. This did good for a time; but when the autumn
drew on, and the weather became more changeable, her mother’s idea of
the unhealthiness of the place increased; and she repined even more
frequently that her husband, who was more learned than Mr. Hume, a
better parish priest than Mr. Houldsworth, should not have met with the
preferment that these two former neighbours of theirs had done.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rich evocation of Helstone setting and Margaret's joy in forest life contrasted with domestic unhappiness; reveals character aspirations and introduces tension between parents.
enrichment.best_quote: She took a pride in her forest. Its people were her people.
enrichment.summary: Margaret thrives in outdoor life at Helstone, befriending locals and immersing herself in nature, but discovers her parents' domestic discontent over Mr. Hale's position and prospects.

text:
This marring of the peace of home, by long hours of discontent, was what
Margaret was unprepared for. She knew, and had rather revelled in the
idea, that she should have to give up many luxuries, which had only been
troubles and trammels to her freedom in Harley Street. Her keen
enjoyment of every sensuous pleasure was balanced finely, if not
overbalanced, by her conscious pride in being able to do without them
all, if need were. But the cloud never comes in that quarter of the
horizon from which we watch for it. There had been slight complaints and
passing regrets on her mother’s part, over some trifle connected with
Helstone, and her father’s position there, when Margaret had been
spending her holidays at home before; but in the general happiness of
the recollection of those times, she had forgotten the small details
which were not so pleasant.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reflects on Margaret's expectations versus reality, noting she is unprepared for domestic unhappiness, though this introduces a recurring theme.
enrichment.best_quote: But the cloud never comes in that quarter of the horizon from which we watch for it.
enrichment.summary: Margaret expected to sacrifice luxuries willingly but was unprepared for her mother's persistent dissatisfaction with Helstone and her father's position.

and Margaret was obliged to remain more in the house than she had
hitherto done. Helstone was at some distance from any neighbours of
their own standard of cultivation.

said Mrs. Hale, in one of her plaintive moods. “I can’t help regretting
constantly that papa has really no one to associate with here; he is so
thrown away; seeing no one but farmers and labourers from week’s end to

in trade at Southampton? Oh! I’m glad we don’t visit them. I don’t like
shoppy people. I think we are far better off, knowing only cottagers
and labourers, and people without pretence.”

secretly thinking of a young and handsome Mr. Gormon whom she had once
met at Mr. Hume’s.

“No! I call mine a very comprehensive taste; I like all people whose
occupations have to do with land; I like soldiers and sailors, and the

“But the Gormons were neither butchers nor bakers, but very respectable
coach-builders.”

enrichment.summary: Mrs. Hale clarifies that the Gormons are coach-builders, not butchers or bakers.

text:
“Very well. Coach-building is a trade all the same, and I think a much
more useless one than that of butchers or bakers. Oh! how tired I used
to be of the drives every day in Aunt Shaw’s carriage, and how I longed
to walk!”
