sweetheart, one of the lingerers added, “Your bonny face, my lass, makes
the day look brighter.” And another day, as she was unconsciously
smiling at some passing thought, she was addressed by a poorly-dressed,
middle-aged workman, with, “You may well smile, my lass; many a one
would smile to have such a bonny face.” This man looked so careworn that
Margaret could not help giving him an answering smile, glad to think
that her looks, such as they were, should have had the power to call up
a pleasant thought. He seemed to understand her acknowledging glance,
and a silent recognition was established between them whenever the
chances of the day brought them across each other’s paths. They had
never exchanged a word; nothing had been said but that first compliment;
yet somehow Margaret looked upon this man with more interest than upon
any one else in Milton. Once or twice, on Sundays, she saw him walking
with a girl, evidently his daughter, and, if possible, still more
unhealthy than he was himself.

father’s regard for Mr. Thornton, to subdue the irritation of weariness

with that friend of Mr. Bell’s; that Mr. Hale?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Thornton's question reveals her knowledge of her son's plans and his social connections, setting up the revelation of his intentions.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Thornton asks why her son has come home early, mentioning his planned tea visit with Mr. Hale.

text: “So I am, mother. I am come home to dress!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: John's brief response that he has come home to dress reveals his care about his appearance for the visit; minor but characterizing detail.
enrichment.summary: John confirms he has come home to dress for his visit.

text:
“Dress! humph! When I was a girl, young men were satisfied with dressing
once in a day. Why should you dress to go and take a cup of tea with an
old parson?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Thornton's dismissal of the custom reveals generational difference and sets up John's defense; comic but reveals maternal attitude.
enrichment.best_quote: When I was a girl, young men were satisfied with dressing once in a day.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Thornton questions why John needs to dress for a mere tea visit with an old parson.

text: “Mr. Hale is a gentleman, and his wife and daughter are ladies.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: John's defense of the Hales as respectable gentry reveals his respect for them and hints at his regard for Margaret.
enrichment.best_quote: Mr. Hale is a gentleman, and his wife and daughter are ladies.
enrichment.summary: John defends the Hales as respectable gentry, implying they deserve proper dress.

text:
“Wife and daughter! Do they teach too? What do they do? You have never
mentioned them.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Thornton's probing questions about Mrs. Hale and Margaret reveal her protective concern and curiosity about potential rivals for her son's attention.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Thornton asks what Mrs. Hale and Miss Hale do, as John has never mentioned them.

text:
“No! mother, because I have never seen Mrs. Hale; I have only seen Miss
Hale for half an hour.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: John's admission reveals limited prior contact with Margaret, contradicting any suggestion of previous familiarity.
enrichment.summary: John clarifies he has never seen Mrs. Hale and has only met Miss Hale once, briefly.

text: “Take care you don’t get caught by a penniless girl, John.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Thornton's warning about being 'caught' by a penniless girl is both comic and suggests her concern about John's romantic vulnerability.
enrichment.best_quote: Take care you don't get caught by a penniless girl, John.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Thornton warns John against being ensnared by a wealthy suitor.

text:
“I am not easily caught, mother, as I think you know. But I must not
have Miss Hale spoken of in that way, which, you know, is offensive to
me. I never was aware of any young lady trying to catch me yet, nor do I
believe that any one has ever given themselves that useless trouble.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: John's firm but respectful rebuke of his mother reveals his protective attitude toward Margaret and his independent judgment; emotionally charged moment.
enrichment.best_quote: I never was aware of any young lady trying to catch me yet, nor do I believe that any one has ever given themselves that useless trouble.
enrichment.summary: John defends himself, insisting he is not easily caught, and demands that his mother not speak disrespectfully of Miss Hale.

text:
Mrs. Thornton did not choose to yield the point to her son; or else she
had, in general, pride enough for her sex.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief narratorial comment on Mrs. Thornton's pride; routine connective observation.
enrichment.summary: The narrator observes that Mrs. Thornton would not yield the point, having pride enough for both sexes.

text:
“Well! I only say, take care. Perhaps our Milton girls have too much
spirit and good feeling to go angling after husbands; but this Miss Hale
comes out of the aristocratic counties, where, if all tales be true,
rich husbands are reckoned prizes.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Thornton's barbed comment about southern wives and their mercenary marriage-hunting reveals class stereotypes and her suspicions about Margaret's intentions.
enrichment.best_quote: Perhaps our Milton girls have too much spirit and good feeling to go angling after husbands; but this Miss Hale comes out of the aristocratic counties, where, if all tales be true, rich husbands are reckoned prizes.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Thornton contrasts virtuous Milton girls with southern aristocratic women, implying Miss Hale may be a fortune-hunter.

text:
Mr. Thornton’s brow contracted, and he came a step forward into the
room.

enrichment.interest_rationale: John's visible reaction to his mother's jibe signals his emotional involvement and defensive posture.
enrichment.summary: John's brow contracts and he moves forward, showing his anger at his mother's insinuation.

text:
“Mother” (with a short scornful laugh), “you will make me confess. The
only time I saw Miss Hale, she treated me with a haughty civility which
had a strong flavour of contempt in it. She held herself aloof from me
as if she had been a queen, and I her humble, unwashed vassal. Be easy,
mother.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: John's revelation of his earlier encounter with Margaret—her haughty disdain—is a pivotal moment that reframes their dynamic and suggests deeper feelings beneath his defensive posture.
enrichment.best_quote: she treated me with a haughty civility which had a strong flavour of contempt in it. She held herself aloof from me as if she had been a queen, and I her humble, unwashed vassal.
enrichment.summary: John confesses to his mother that when he met Margaret, she treated him with contempt and disdain, holding herself aloof as a queen dismissing a vassal.

text:
“No! I am not easy nor content either. What business had she, a renegade
clergyman’s daughter, to turn up her nose at you! I would dress for none
of them—a saucy set! if I were you.” As he was leaving the room he
said:—

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Thornton's indignant response reveals her fierce maternal pride and contempt for the Hales, while John's calm departure shows his control and private feeling.
enrichment.best_quote: What business had she, a renegade clergyman's daughter, to turn up her nose at you!
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Thornton indignantly defends her son against Margaret's supposed insult; John responds calmly and leaves, promising to describe Mrs. Hale later.

text:
“Mr. Hale is good, and gentle, and learned. He is not saucy. As for Mrs.
Hale, I will tell you what she is like to-night, if you care to hear.”
He shut the door, and was gone.

enrichment.interest_rationale: John's dignified defense of Mr. Hale and promise to describe Mrs. Hale shows his respect for the family and his measured temperament.
enrichment.best_quote: Mr. Hale is good, and gentle, and learned.
enrichment.summary: John praises Mr. Hale's character and offers to describe Mrs. Hale to his mother later, then exits.

text:
“Despise my son! treat him as her vassal, indeed! Humph! I should like
to know where she could find such another! Boy and man, he’s the
noblest, stoutest heart I ever knew. I don’t care if I am his mother; I
can see what’s what, and not be blind. I know what Fanny is; and I know
what John is. Despise him! I hate her!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Thornton's passionate soliloquy about her son's nobility reveals her fierce maternal love, her contempt for Margaret, and her single-minded devotion to John; a powerful character study.
enrichment.best_quote: Boy and man, he's the noblest, stoutest heart I ever knew. I don't care if I am his mother; I can see what's what, and not be blind.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Thornton passionately defends her son's merit to herself, expressing hatred for Margaret and pride in John's character.
